item.title: Sri Lanka Cabinet approves Rs.500bn worth projects amid criticism over spending
item.dc:creator: Shihar Aneez
item.description: Government has spent less than 25% of allocated 2026 capital spending in first nine months
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s Cabinet of Ministers approved a raft of infrastructure projects worth nearly Rs. 500 billion, Cabinet Spokesman Nalinda Jayatissa said on Tuesday, amid growing criticism over unspent capital spending allocated in 2026 budget.

The Cabinet approved Rs. 251.4 billion worth of projects to construct the road section of the first phase of the Ruwanpura Expressway from Kahatuduwa to Ingiriya, including the system interchange.

It also approved Rs. 243.44 billion worth of projects to construct the road section from Kurunegala to Galewela as the first stage of the fourth section from Kurunegala to Dambulla of the Central Expressway Project.

The approvals come amid growing criticism against the government over the timely spending of capital investment.

As per Treasury officials, the government has spent only less than 25 percent of the total allocated Rs. 1,380 billion in capital expenditure in the first nine months of this year.

The government acknowledged the delay and cited lingering approval and procurement processes as the reason.

It said a new advanced approval and procurement process has been planned for 2027, for which the government has allocated a record Rs. 2,000 billion for capital expenditure.

On Monday, opposition legislator Harsha de Silva told parliament that the government has been unable to spend money for projects citing grassroots-level anecdotal evidence of a smart classroom.

“The treasury has been collectingmoney  through tax after tax, but the government has failed to spend it and create jobs,” de Silva said. (Colombo/November 17/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka Telecom accelerates shift to tech company with AI, 5G, and data center push
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: “We want to be a new-age technology company, a techco, and move away from traditional telco,”
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka Telecom (SLT-Mobitel) is accelerating its shift from a traditional telecom operator into a technology company, prioritizing artificial intelligence, targeted 5G expansion, and data centers after posting strong profit growth in the first nine months of 2026.

The state-run group said it is moving beyond legacy voice and connectivity services into digital products to counter rising competition from global over-the-top (OTT) platforms.

“We want to be a new-age technology company, a techco, and move away from traditional telco,” SLT-Mobitel Chairman Mothilal de Silva told reporters.

Having recently launched South Asia’s first smart AI token platform — which allows users to access ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini and has already attracted over 14,000 users — the company plans to expand the service to general consumers and small businesses through new partnerships.

It will also scale up its AI Hub for local developers, enterprises, and students.

On network infrastructure, SLT-Mobitel plans to expand its 4G, fiber, and 5G footprint alongside data centers and international carrier services.

Unlike past industry rollouts, the group said its upcoming 5G investments will target areas with high device penetration to conserve US dollars and maximize returns.

“We will not waste a single dollar on idle towers. Every 5G base station we deploy will serve real customers with real demand,” de Silva said.

The group is also working to finish connecting all 6,225 secondary schools with fiber, having completed 71 percent so far, before expanding connectivity to primary schools and other state institutions.

Internally, SLT and Mobitel are restructuring operations to cut costs.

The expansion is supported by an improved balance sheet. Group profit after tax rose 59 percent year-on-year to 10.3 billion rupees in the first nine months of 2026, matching full-year 2025 earnings, as revenue grew 11 percent to 94 billion rupees.

Mobitel’s third-quarter net profit nearly tripled to 1.8 billion rupees.

Having retired billions of rupees in expensive foreign debt early and earned a Fitch Ratings upgrade to AA+, SLT-Mobitel said it will self-fund its upcoming investments without relying on state bailouts. (Colombo/Nov17/2026)

item.title: UAE-based firms win US$12mn worth SriLankan jet fuel supply contracts
item.dc:creator: Shihar Aneez
item.description: The two UAE-based companies won the contracts among eight bidders
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Two companies based in the United Arab Emirates won contracts to supply jet fuel worth US$ 12 million for SriLankan Airlines flights in four airports for more than two years, a Cabinet document showed.

Both World Fuel Services Trading DMCC (WFS) and Aviation Services Management FZE (ASM) won the contracts in a competitive bidding to supply jet fuel for SriLankan Airlines.

World Fuel Services Trading DMCC won contracts to supply aircraft fuel for 25 months starting from December 1, 2026, in Incheon Airport in South Korea for US$ 240,021 and Frankfurt Airport in Germany for US$ 293,456.

Aviation Services Management FZE won the contracts to supply jet fuel for SriLankan Airlines in India’s Ahmadabad Airport for US$ 5.95 million starting from November 15, 2026 through end 2028.

ASM also succeeded in winning US$6.48 million contract in Pakistan’s Lahore Airport to supply jet fuel for 23 months from December 1, 2026.

Cabinet Spokesman Nalinda Jayatissa said Eight bids were received and based on the recommendations submitted by the Higher Level Standing Procurement Committee, the Cabinet approved awarding the contracts as follows to the substantially responsive minimum bidders.

World Fuel Services Trading DMCC (WFS) is registered in the United Arab Emirates, specializing in the procurement and global distribution of refined petroleum products.

Aviation Services Management FZE is a global flight support provider headquartered in Dubai. (Colombo/November 17/2026)

item.title: Seven new envoys present credentials to Sri Lanka President
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: South Korea, Switzerland, European Union, Egypt, Laos, Namibia, and Singapore
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Seven newly appointed Ambassadors-designate and High Commissioners-designate presented their Letters of Credence to President Anura Kumara Dissanayake at the Presidential Secretariat today (17), his media division said.

The newly appointed envoys are:
1. Kim Youn-Jung, Ambassador-designate of the Republic of Korea, based in Colombo.
2. Daniel Hunn, Ambassador-designate of Switzerland, based in Colombo.
3. Sylvia Hartleif, Ambassador-designate of the European Union, based in Colombo.
4. Ahmed El-Sayed Abdel Halim Amer Helal, Ambassador-designate of the Arab Republic of Egypt, based in Colombo.
5. Vithaya Xayavong, Ambassador-designate of the Lao People’s Democratic Republic, based in New Delhi.
6. Wing Commander Alex L. Tukuhupwele (Retd.), High Commissioner-designate of the Republic of Namibia, based in New Delhi.
7. Patrick Daniel, High Commissioner-designate of the Republic of Singapore, based in Singapore.

The governments of the Republic of Korea, Switzerland, the Arab Republic of Egypt, the Lao People’s Democratic Republic, the Republic of Namibia and the Republic of Singapore, as well as the European Union, had appointed the above envoys to represent them in Sri Lanka, with the agreement of the Government of Sri Lanka.

Meanwhile, Sri Lanka is yet to appoint Ambassadors and High Commissioners to the United States, Seychelles, Kenya, Canada, Jordan, Germany, and China. (Colombo/Nov17/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka’s CSE penalizes Laugfs Gas for annual report delay
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: Firm is also facing litigation brought against it by country's Consumer Affairs Authority for not ensuring gas supply
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – The Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE) has imposed a penalty on Laugfs Gas PLC for failing to submit its annual report for the financial year ended March 31, 2026, on time.

The exchange said in a market filing Tuesday that the company had failed to ensure timely compliance with Rule 7.5.1 (A) (1) of the CSE Listing Rules, which requires listed entities to circulate annual reports within five months of their financial year-end.

Following the non-compliance, the CSE required Laugfs Gas to provide reasons for the delay under Rule 7.5.3 (A) (4) (a).

However, the exchange said the explanation provided by the company could not be considered a valid justification to warrant a deviation from the rule.

The regulatory action comes amid mounting financial and legal pressures at the energy firm.

Last week, Laugfs Gas reported a group net loss of 1.54 billion rupees for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, widening 88 percent from a loss of 818.2 million rupees a year earlier, after group revenue plunged 57 percent to 5.71 billion rupees.

The firm is also facing litigation brought against it by the country’s Consumer Affairs Authority for not ensuring continuous gas supply.

The liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) supplier has said it is discussing options with interested parties involving its wholly owned subsidiary, LAUGFS Terminals Limited, which owns and operates a 30,000-tonne LPG terminal at the Hambantota International Port.

The discussions include commercial collaborations, investments, and the possible disposal of part or all of its shareholding in the subsidiary, the listed company said in the market filing.

Vallibel Three (Pvt) Ltd, controlled by billionaire Dammika Perera, owns 50 percent of Laugfs Holdings.(Colombo/Nov17/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka stocks slide 0.27-pct on profit-taking
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: The CSE saw upward momentum, surpassing the 22,000 mark, ahead of the country's national budget presentation last we
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s bourse dipped 0.27 percent on Tuesday, amidst some profit-taking at the Colombo Stock Exchange ahead of the upcoming monetary policy announcement, brokers said.

“The market is a bit volatile following a very good run as there is some profit-taking,” Ranjan Ranatunga, Assistant Vice President – Research at First Capital said.

“There’s also some indecisiveness ahead of the monetary policy meeting.”

Market turnover was 3.73 billion rupees.

The All Share Price Index was down 58.82 points at 21,673.55; while the S&P SL20 was down 0.23 percent, or 14.40 points, at 6,185.

The top positive contributors to the ASPI were Vallibel One (up 1.20 rupees at 93.80), C T Holdings (up 16.25 rupees at 566.25), and Lion Brewery (up 27.25 rupees at 1,927.75).

The top negative contributors were Commercial Bank (down 2.25 rupees at 219.50), Carson Cumberbatch (down 9.75 rupees at 698.00), and Hatton National Bank (down 1.75 rupees at 398.00).

The CSE saw upward momentum, surpassing the 22,000 mark, ahead of the country’s national budget presentation last week.

It has since slid, even as the National People’s Power government’s third budget is being debated in parliament over the month. (Colombo/Nov17/2026)

item.title: EXPLAINER – What does NVIDIA’s Huang scandal mean for Sri Lanka?
item.dc:creator: Shihar Aneez
item.description: Sri Lanka's vital IT, BPO, banking, telcos rely on cloud platforms, software services powered by NVIDIA hardware
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – In the span of three turbulent weeks this November, the global technology sector witnessed the stunning unraveling of its most celebrated architect.

Jensen Huang, the leather-jacketed visionary who spent 33 years building NVIDIA from a niche graphics card maker into a multi-trillion-dollar artificial intelligence colossus, resigned abruptly as chief executive, president, and board member on November 12, 2026.

His departure, triggered by a volatile collision of personal infidelity, workplace governance failures, and alleged foreign espionage, has sent shock waves from Silicon Valley to Colombo, raising urgent questions about national security, data confidentiality, and the fragility of the global AI supply chain.

The crisis began in late October when The New York Times revealed that U.S. intelligence agencies were investigating an extramarital affair between Huang and Alice Huang (not related to Jensen), also known as Huang Le, a Chinese businesswoman and former controlling shareholder of Singapore-based cloud firm Megaspeed International.

American intelligence officials suspected Alice Huang of acting as an asset for China’s Ministry of State Security, even as regulators in Singapore and Malaysia were already scrutinizing Megaspeed over suspected false server declarations and the illicit diversion of restricted AI chips to China.

Though Jensen Huang initially dismissed the reports and insisted his interactions were strictly commercial, mounting evidence forced him to issue a public apology on November 8 admitting infidelity.

Days later, subsequent revelations uncovered two additional secret relationships with NVIDIA subordinates, including Vice President of Healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him.

It was not immediately clear if the secret relationships were deliberate honey traps.

Facing a board-led investigation and intense congressional scrutiny, Jensen Huang stepped down, leaving Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO and venture capitalist Harvey C. Jones as the company’s first-ever independent board chair.

Breach of Trust

Beyond the salacious headlines, the scandal represents a profound breach of corporate and fiduciary trust.

By conducting concealed romantic relationships with direct reports, Jenson Huang undermined fundamental workplace governance, creating severe conflicts of interest over promotions, compensation, and executive influence.

Worse still, his initial denial followed by a belated confession shattered the credibility of a leader long admired as a steady, disciplined family man.

Questions also linger over commercial judgment: between late 2023 and 2024, Megaspeed’s assets ballooned nearly ninety-fold to roughly $3 billion as it snapped up advanced NVIDIA hardware, casting a harsh light on whether personal entanglements compromised NVIDIA’s compliance oversight.

For Washington, the affair struck straight at the heart of U.S. national security.

Frontier AI accelerators such as NVIDIA’s Hopper and Blackwell architectures are viewed by defence planners as strategic assets vital to military superiority and cyber dominance, protected by strict export controls designed to keep them out of Beijing’s hands.

Intelligence officials view Jensen Huang’s entanglement through the prism of a classic influence operation.

Even if no classified blueprints ever changed hands, proximity to a suspected foreign intelligence operative created an acute vulnerability to blackmail, subtle policy influence, particularly given Huang’s frequent lobbying against stringent U.S. chip restrictions, and visibility into supply chain loopholes across Southeast Asia.

Hero to Zero

The fallout has injected immediate turbulence into the global artificial intelligence industry.

Huang commanded an extraordinary “founder premium,” serving as both chief strategist and chief evangelist of the AI revolution.

His exit wiped hundreds of billions of dollars off NVIDIA’s market value and rattled global tech indices.

While the company’s immediate hardware road map through 2028 remains intact, long-term architectural bets, massive ecosystem investments, and developer confidence face renewed uncertainty.

Meanwhile, U.S. lawmakers and the Treasury Department are preparing aggressive compliance audits and tighter “Know Your Customer” rules for cloud operators worldwide, creating a rare strategic opening for rivals like AMD, Broadcom, and custom silicon programs at Google, Amazon, and Microsoft.

Equally troubling are the implications for the confidentiality of chip users.

Global enterprises, governments, and researchers rely on NVIDIA GPUs and its proprietary CUDA software stack to train models on their most sensitive proprietary data.

Security analysts warn of two distinct risks: first, that any foreign intelligence insight into NVIDIA’s internal firmware or engineering road maps could aid adversaries in discovering subtle hardware or side-channel vulnerabilities.

The second is businesses renting compute capacity through opaque third-party Asian cloud brokers risk having sensitive workloads routed onto compromised or legally imperiled infrastructure.

Impact on Sri Lanka

While Sri Lanka sits thousands of miles from Santa Clara, neither local enterprises nor everyday citizens are insulated from the aftershocks.

Global corporations face immediate supply chain audits and delayed GPU allocations, and Sri Lankan businesses, particularly across the country’s vital IT, Business Process Outsourcing, banking, and telecommunications sectors, rely heavily on hyper scale cloud platforms and regional software services powered by NVIDIA hardware.

Tighter U.S. export scrutiny across South and Southeast Asia threatens to drive up cloud compute costs, lengthen procurement timelines for local data centers, and impose stricter security compliance hurdles on Sri Lankan tech firms serving Western clients.

For individual Sri Lankans, software engineers, startup founders, freelancers, and everyday digital consumers, the stakes are personal as well as economic.

Sri Lanka’s digital export economy thrives on trust from North American and European clients; heightened regional compliance barriers could make winning international contracts more complex and costly.

At the same time, rising global compute prices inevitably trickle down into more expensive AI subscriptions and tighter cloud credits for local developers and universities, while any disruption or compromise in regional cloud hubs directly affects the reliability and privacy of fintech, telecom, and consumer AI apps used daily across the island.

Navigating these risks requires swift, coordinated precautions across Sri Lanka’s public and private sectors.

Regulators such as the Telecommunications Regulatory Commission of Sri Lanka (TRCSL) and Sri Lanka CERT must audit cross-border cloud routing to ensure government and critical infrastructure data remain hosted strictly within Tier-1, independently audited cloud regions with enforceable data residency guarantees.

The customs authorities also should tighten trade oversight to prevent Sri Lanka from ever being exploited as a transshipment point for restricted hardware.

Simultaneously, Sri Lankan banks and enterprises must audit third-party AI vendors for ISO 27001 and SOC 2 compliance and deploy hardware-level confidential computing, which keeps sensitive data encrypted even while being processed inside GPU memory.

Developers and citizens should adopt model-agnostic software architectures and refrain from uploading sensitive personal or corporate records into unverified AI platforms.

Ultimately, the downfall of Jensen Huang serves as a sobering parable for the modern technological era.

No founder, regardless of the trillions in value they create, is too indispensable for rigorous board oversight; concentrating unchecked authority in a single executive without an independent chair invites systemic fragility.

More starkly, in strategic industries such as semiconductors and artificial intelligence, personal conduct is no longer a private matter, unmanaged human vulnerabilities rapidly become geopolitical attack surfaces.

As Sri Lanka and the wider world build their economic futures atop AI infrastructure, the crisis underscores one enduring truth: rapid innovation cannot outrun compliance, and true resilience demands diversification rather than dependence on any single leader, vendor, or supply chain. (Colombo/November 17/2026)

item.title: Janashakthi PLC posts Rs662mn Sept quarter net loss amid market volatility
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: Earnings were weighed down by supply-side shocks
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT — Sri Lanka financial services group Janashakthi PLC (JXG) recorded a net loss attributable to equity holders of Rs. 662.3 million for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, swinging from a net profit of Rs. 484.0 million a year earlier, interim accounts showed.

Annualised basic loss per share stood at Rs. 1.20 for the September quarter, compared to earnings per share of Rs. 1.10 in the same period last year.

Quarterly revenue declined 9.9 percent to Rs. 6.57 billion from Rs. 7.29 billion a year ago, though top-line performance improved sequentially by about 3 percent from the June quarter as capital market conditions began stabilizing.

Earnings were weighed down by supply-side shocks from the conflict in West Asia, which pushed up monetary policy rates, inflation, and capital market volatility.

This hit investment returns at primary dealer First Capital Treasuries PLC and parent First Capital Holdings PLC, as well as mark-to-market valuations at Janashakthi Insurance PLC — which is consolidated with a three-month lag using June 30 figures — offsetting resilient loan and deposit growth at Janashakthi Finance PLC.

Cost of sales and direct expenses rose 4.1 percent to Rs. 5.32 billion, reducing gross profit by 42.9 percent to Rs. 1.25 billion.

Fair value losses on financial assets narrowed 69.1 percent to Rs. 264.5 million and administrative expenses fell 11.0 percent to Rs. 1.76 billion, but impairment charges surged 178.4 percent to Rs. 149.7 million, widening operating losses to Rs. 802.2 million.

Finance income dropped 59.4 percent to Rs. 947.4 million while finance costs increased 18.2 percent to Rs. 623.6 million amid higher borrowings and repurchase liabilities.

The accounts reported no impact from exchange rate depreciation, reflecting the group’s predominantly domestic rupee-denominated operations.

After income tax expenses of Rs. 201.2 million, total group net loss stood at Rs. 679.6 million, compared to a profit of Rs. 894.5 million previously.

JXG signed an agreement on August 13 with Melstacorp PLC to acquire 100 percent of Continental Insurance Lanka Limited for Rs. 5.2 billion in stages — subject to regulatory approval — marking its re-entry into general insurance.

Following its Rs. 5 billion initial public offering, the group also appointed a dedicated chief executive to launch a microfinance business and an officer to spearhead overseas expansion.

Total assets rose 17.7 percent from March to Rs. 184.56 billion as of September 30, with net asset value per share at Rs. 6.00.

Janashakthi PLC shares closed at Rs. 10.00 at the end of September and are currently trading around Rs. 9.60.  (Colombo/Nov17/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka rubber traders warn of structural bottlenecks as industry turns 150
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: Sri Lanka rubber industry at 150 faces structural threats, the Colombo Rubber Traders’ Association (CRTA) warn
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – As Sri Lanka’s rubber industry marks 150 years of natural rubber cultivation, the Colombo Rubber Traders’ Association (CRTA) warns that the sector’s future is threatened unless the government addresses critical structural bottlenecks.

“This anniversary must be more than a celebration of our past. It must serve as a renewed commitment to revitalizing the industry, addressing the challenges confronting our stakeholders and securing a commercially sustainable, competitive and prosperous future for Sri Lankan natural rubber,” Harin de Silva, Chairman of the Colombo Rubber Traders’ Association (CRTA), said.

The arrival of Hevea brasiliensis seedlings at the Henarathgoda Botanical Gardens in Gampaha in 1876 marked the beginning of a journey that would establish Sri Lanka among the pioneering nations of the Asian natural rubber industry, CRTA said.

Rubber evolved into an agricultural commodity, a cornerstone of rural livelihoods and an essential raw material supporting a wide range of industries across the world.

“Celebrating 150 years of Sri Lanka’s natural rubber industry is an occasion of immense pride for our nation. It is a tribute to the generations of rubber tappers, smallholders, plantation companies, estate managers, researchers, processors, brokers, traders and exporters whose dedication, knowledge and enterprise have built an industry of international significance,” de Silva said.

Sri Lanka was among the earliest Asian countries to benefit from the expansion of commercial rubber cultivation, eventually developing an industry recognized for its technical expertise, product quality and contribution to international commerce.

The establishment of the Rubber Research Institute of Sri Lanka in 1909, recognized as the world’s oldest rubber research institute, further strengthened this foundation, supporting advances in cultivation, processing, productivity and product development.

Sri Lanka’s long-standing expertise in premium natural rubber grades, particularly its renowned latex crepe grades, remains an important part of this.

The 1952 Rubber-Rice Pact with China also stands as a defining chapter in the country’s economic history, demonstrating how natural rubber could serve not only as a source of export earnings but also as an instrument of international cooperation and economic diplomacy.

The strength of the rubber industry has always depended on the collective efforts of agricultural producers, scientific institutions, commercial enterprises and international partners.

The CRTA, which represents the interests of the natural rubber trading community, says traders have historically served as an essential link between brokers, producers, processors, manufacturers and international markets.

“Rubber trading is not merely the buying and selling of a commodity. It involves financing, sourcing, quality assurance, market intelligence, logistics, risk management and the development of long-standing relationships with overseas buyers.”

For more than 116 years, the Weekly Colombo Rubber Auction has served as a cornerstone of Sri Lanka’s natural rubber trade, providing an established marketplace that brings together producers, brokers, traders and buyers.

Traders continue to play a vital role in connecting the output of smallholders and plantations with domestic manufacturers and global supply chains, ensuring that Sri Lankan natural rubber reaches markets both locally and internationally.

“A strong and commercially viable trading sector is therefore indispensable to the sustainability of the wider industry. When traders are able to operate within a predictable, transparent and competitive business environment, they are better positioned to support producers, maintain reliable supplies, invest in new opportunities and secure markets for Sri Lankan rubber.”

Sri Lanka’s natural rubber industry faces significant challenges, CRTA said, that require urgent and coordinated attention.

Declining or stagnant productivity in many traditional growing areas, ageing rubber trees, rising production costs, labor constraints, insufficient replanting, lack of effective rain-guarding systems across many rubber-growing areas and the need to bring underutilized land back into productive use all place pressure on the industry’s long-term viability.

Smallholders, who form an important part of the production base, require support to ensure that rubber cultivation remains an attractive and economically sustainable livelihood.

An equally important consideration is the need to provide long-term investment certainty to Regional Plantation Companies (RPCs), CRTA says, whose existing land lease agreements are due to expire in 2045.

The CRTA says the extension of these lease agreements is essential to safeguarding the future of the plantation sector.

“Providing clarity and certainty on the long-term tenure of these lands would encourage RPCs to undertake the substantial investments required for replanting, improving productivity, modernizing infrastructure, adopting sustainable plantation management practices and developing the full commercial potential of their estates.

“Without such certainty, the willingness and capacity of plantation companies to commit to long-term investments could be adversely affected, with implications for the sustainability of the wider rubber industry.”

Sri Lanka must also look beyond its traditional rubber-growing regions and explore opportunities to expand cultivation into suitable, drier, non-traditional areas of the country, the traders body said.

With appropriate research, climate suitability assessments, land-use planning and the development of suitable planting material and agronomic practices, such expansion could help diversify the country’s rubber production base, reduce its geographical concentration in traditional wet-zone areas and create new opportunities to increase domestic natural rubber production.

This would also provide an opportunity to bring suitable underutilised land into productive agricultural use while strengthening the industry’s resilience to changing climatic conditions.

International competition, price volatility, changing patterns of industrial demand and increasingly stringent environmental and supply-chain requirements are reshaping the global rubber trade.

Compliance with the European Union Deforestation Regulation (EUDR), including applicable traceability and geo-location requirements, illustrates the growing importance of demonstrating the origin and sustainability of natural rubber supplied to international markets.

These challenges cannot be resolved by any single stakeholder or institution, CRTA pointed out, but needs a coordinated approach involving the Government, the Rubber Research Institute of Sri Lanka, the Rubber Development Department, plantation companies, smallholder organizations, processors, brokers, traders, exporters and manufacturers.

The CRTA says the industry’s revitalization must be driven by practical measures that improve productivity, strengthen the economics of cultivation, encourage replanting, facilitate access to quality planting material, modernize processing and improve market access.

“Equally important is the need to strengthen collaboration between the public and private sectors, ensure that policies reflect the commercial realities faced by industry participants and create an environment that encourages long-term investment.”

Sri Lanka’s established capabilities in rubber-based manufacturing, including its internationally recognized position as “the world’s solid tire manufacturing capital”, alongside its production of surgical gloves, latex bedding and other industrial and specialized rubber products, demonstrate the country’s capacity to create greater value from natural rubber.

“Building on these strengths will be vital to expanding value-added manufacturing, strengthening global competitiveness and increasing the contribution of the wider rubber industry to the national economy.”

The CRTA encourages continued investment in technology, product innovation, quality improvement and the development of new export markets.

Closer collaboration between rubber producers, traders, research institutions and manufacturers can help ensure the country’s natural rubber is channeled towards applications that reward quality, consistency and technical performance.

“Sri Lanka must also continue to protect and promote the distinctive qualities of its premium rubber grades, including latex crepe grades, while responding to the evolving requirements of international customers,” the Chairman said.

“A competitive industry will depend not only on producing more rubber, but also on producing it efficiently, maintaining consistent quality, meeting international standards and delivering products that create sustainable value for all participants in the supply chain,” he said.

The next phase of the industry’s development must place sustainability and responsible sourcing at its center.

Improved plantation management, higher yields from existing cultivated areas, effective replanting programs, appropriate land-use planning and stronger traceability systems can contribute to both environmental responsibility and commercial resilience.

For exporters and traders, the ability to provide reliable information whilst complying with compliance protocols such as the European Union Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) on the origin and movement of rubber will increasingly influence access to international markets.

Industry-wide cooperation is therefore essential to help growers, smallholders, processors and other supply-chain participants meet applicable regulatory requirements without undermining their commercial viability.

The CRTA called for practical technical assistance, coordinated data collection, clear guidance and proportionate implementation support to help the industry adapt to these evolving requirements.

“Sustainability must be treated not simply as a regulatory obligation, but as an opportunity to strengthen Sri Lanka’s reputation as a reliable supplier of quality natural rubber,” de Silva said.

The CRTA said a revitalized Sri Lankan rubber industry should be built on five priorities: improving productivity and replanting; strengthening the economic viability of smallholders and plantations; enhancing research, innovation and value addition; improving supply-chain transparency and regulatory readiness; and reinforcing the competitiveness of Sri Lankan rubber in international markets.

“Our responsibility is to ensure that rubber remains a viable livelihood for our growers, a dependable source of business for our traders, a competitive raw material for our manufacturers and a trusted product for our international customers,” de Silva said. (Colombo/Nov17/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka stocks trend higher, ASPI up 0.37-pct
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: Positive contributors to the ASPI were Distilleries, Dialog, Vallibel One, Singer and Asiri Hospital

Hatton National Bank (down 0.19 percent at 399 rupees), Sunshine Holdings (down 1.29 percent at 30.50 rupees), WealthTrust Securities (down 2.48 percent at 11.80 rupees), and Citizens Development Business Finance (down 0.89 percent at 33.50 rupees) were top negative contributors.

Market turnover was 258.27 million rupees. Capital goods led turnover with 120.69 million rupees. (Colombo/Nov17/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka rupee at 332.80/88 to US dollar spot, bond yields lower
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: Bond yields were quoted steady to lower, dealers said.
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s rupee was quoted at 332.80/88 to the US dollar spot on Tuesday, weaker from 332.75/85 the previous day, while bond yields were quoted steady to lower, dealers said.

item.title: Sri Lanka services expands at higher rate in October 2026: PMI
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: Driven by improvements in other personal services, with notable contributions from financial services and goods transpor
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s services sector expanded at a higher rate in October 2026, according to a Purchasing Managers Index compiled by the central bank, which registered an index value of 62.5, compared to 60.5 the previous month.

“Business Activity expanded, driven primarily by improvements in other personal services, with notable contributions from financial services and goods transportation,” CBSL said.

New businesses increased at a slower rate in October 2026, registering 59.8 from September’s 60.9, reflecting expansions in financial services and other personal services, alongside positive contributions from accommodation, food and beverage services, and transportation of goods.

Employment increased in October, “supported by recruitment across several sub sectors to meet rising operational requirements”.

Backlogs of Work declined in the month, at a higher rate compared to the previous month.

Expectations for Business Activity over the next three months remained positive, CBSL said, supported by anticipated increases in tourist arrivals, and the upcoming festive season.

“However, prevailing global uncertainties continue to pose downside risks to the outlook.” (Colombo/Nov16/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka manufacturing PMI expands in October, driven by anticipated seasonal demand
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: The New Orders sub-index expanded in driven by the manufacture of textiles and wearing apparel and the food and beverage
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s manufacturing sector expanded in October 2026, registering a value of 55.3 on a Purchasing Managers Index compiled by the central bank, from 53.0 the previous month.

“This expansion was broad-based, with all sub-indices remaining above the neutral threshold,” CBSL said, noting the outlook remains favourable, underpinned by anticipated demand during the upcoming festive season.

The New Orders sub-index expanded in the month, registering 52.2, driven by the manufacture of textiles and wearing apparel and the food and beverages sectors, reflecting seasonal demand.

The Production sub-index registered 51.0, driven by seasonal demand in the textiles and wearing apparel sector.

The Employment sub-index expanded at a slower rate, registering 51.1, from the previous 52.6.

The Stock of Purchases sub-index also expanded from the neutral threshold, registering 56.1.

Suppliers’ Delivery Times sub-index further lengthened during the period, reflecting increased demand for inputs. (Colombo/Nov16/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka stocks close down 1.32-pct amid profit-taking
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: Turnover Rs10.48bn
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s Colombo Stock Exchange closed down on Monday, CSE data showed, with the benchmark All Share Price Index moving down 1.32 percent.

The ASPI was down 291.81 points at 21,732.37, while the more liquid S&P SL20 was down 1.50 percent, or 94.69 points, at 6,199.03.

“More than the budget, what we need to factor in is that the market had been going at a very rapid pace for quite some time,” Raynal Wickremeratne, Head of Research and Strategy at NDB Securities, said.

“Every time the market moves at that speed, there tends to be a period where things slow down a little bit and there is some profit-taking. You actually need a few corrections to have a healthy market.”

Positive contributors to the ASPI were Carson Cumberbatch (up 0.35 percent at 707.75 rupees), Bukit Darah (up 0.53 percent at 859.50 rupees), Citizens Development Business Finance (up 0.90 percent at 33.80 rupees), HNB Life (up 2.19 percent at 140 rupees), and InsureMe Insurance Brokers (up 11.12 percent at 3,045.25 rupees).

Commercial Bank (down 1.55 percent at 221.75 rupees), Dialog Axiata (down 1.20 percent at 49.60 rupees), Hatton National Bank (down 0.99 percent at 399.75 rupees), Tokyo Cement Company (Lanka) (down 4.99 percent at 83.80 rupees), and LOLC Finance (down 5.77 percent at 4.90 rupees) were top negative contributors.

Market turnover was 10.48 billion rupees. Food and staples retailing led turnover with 4.51 billion rupees.

Turnover was bolstered by a major on-board transaction of 4.4 billion rupees in Carson Cumberbatch, alongside several crossings. The largest crossing was recorded in Convenience Foods (Lanka) at 3.976 billion rupees, followed by Dialog Axiata (140 million rupees), Hemas Holdings (41 million rupees), Prime Lands Residencies (30 million rupees), and Aitken Spence (22 million rupees).

Wickremeratne noted that seeing two major transactions in the 4 billion rupee range alongside strong overall turnover was positive for the market. (Colombo/Nov16/2026)

item.title: Softlogic Holdings Sept quarter net loss narrows 25-pct to Rs2.1bn
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: Healthcare anchored earnings, with revenue rising 24 percent to Rs. 10.64 billion and pre-tax profit jumping 80 percent
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT — Sri Lanka conglomerate Softlogic Holdings PLC recorded a net loss attributable to equity holders of Rs. 2.10 billion for the quarter ended September 30, narrowing 25 percent from a loss of Rs. 2.79 billion a year earlier, interim accounts showed.

Basic loss per share improved to Rs. 1.50 from Rs. 2.00 in the same quarter last year.

Quarterly revenue rose 15 percent to Rs. 34.85 billion from Rs. 30.17 billion, outpacing a 12 percent rise in cost of sales to Rs. 22.25 billion and lifting gross profit 22 percent to Rs. 12.60 billion.

Operating profit surged 97 percent to Rs. 3.62 billion, with EBITDA climbing 68 percent to Rs. 4.59 billion, supported by tight administrative expense growth of 3 percent (Rs. 8.17 billion) despite a 27 percent rise in distribution costs to Rs. 1.46 billion.

Healthcare anchored earnings, with revenue rising 24 percent to Rs. 10.64 billion and pre-tax profit jumping 80 percent to Rs. 2.49 billion on higher finance income.

Retail revenue grew 22 percent to Rs. 9.52 billion, though Rs. 1.71 billion in finance costs widened its pre-tax loss to Rs. 2.03 billion.

Information technology swung to a Rs. 181.3 million pre-tax profit and leisure pre-tax losses narrowed 88 percent to Rs. 79.5 million, while automobile revenue fell 57 percent to Rs. 494.6 million.

Financial services revenue increased 15 percent to Rs. 11.76 billion with operating profit up 11 percent to Rs. 1.22 billion, but the segment posted a Rs. 365.7 million pre-tax loss (versus a Rs. 1.28 billion profit previously) after insurance contract liability charges jumped 194 percent to Rs. 2.81 billion.

Notes showed no life insurance surplus was transferred to shareholders during the quarter, compared to Rs. 1.26 billion a year earlier.

Group net finance costs fell 17 percent to Rs. 1.26 billion following Rs. 2.03 billion in rights issue debt repayments. Currency translation of foreign operations had minimal impact, yielding a Rs. 3.19 million gain alongside a Rs. 242.2 million derivative fair value gain.

After Rs. 937.4 million in taxes, total group loss narrowed 7 percent to Rs. 1.40 billion.

Total assets stood at Rs. 212.86 billion with negative net asset value of Rs. 51.36 per share and Rs. 7.63 billion in capital commitments, while subsidiary Asiri Surgical continues litigating a Rs. 1.20 billion BOI tax dispute.

Post-quarter, Softlogic Finance approved a Rs. 1.00 billion rights issue to expand vehicle financing, Softlogic Life announced plans to amalgamate Softlogic Life Insurance Lanka from January 1, 2027, and the parent extended warrant conversion payments to November 19.

Softlogic Holdings’ shares closed at 7.10 rupees at the end of September. The share is currently trading around 9.60 rupees.  (Colombo/Nov16/2026)

item.title: South Korea, Sri Lanka discuss ageing populations, investment
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: Declining fertility rates and a rapidly ageing population that threaten future dependency ratios and workforce availabil
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – A visiting South Korean parliamentary delegation has held talks with Sri Lanka’s Deputy Speaker Rizvie Salih on tackling demographic shifts, climate resilience, and boosting corporate participation ahead of the 50th anniversary of diplomatic relations in 2027.

The delegation from the National Assembly of the Republic of Korea, representing the Korean Parliamentary League on Children, Population and Environment (CPE), committed to encouraging greater participation by Korean enterprises in Sri Lanka’s forthcoming international expo scheduled for January next year, a parliament statement said.

Led by Lee Yang-soo, Chairperson of the National Assembly Intelligence Committee and Vice President of the CPE, the delegation also invited Sri Lanka’s parliament to attend the Asia-Pacific Parliamentarians’ Conference on Environment and Development (APPCED) in South Korea next year.

Both sides noted that natural disasters can undermine years of economic progress and stressed the need to balance environmental protection with economic growth.

Salih flagged Sri Lanka’s own demographic pressures, pointing to declining fertility rates and a rapidly ageing population that threaten future dependency ratios and workforce availability, alongside challenges in sustaining the country’s free education system.

The Korean lawmakers shared South Korea’s policy interventions aimed at reversing low birth rates, including affordable rental housing for newlyweds, low-interest loans, and housing incentives.

They also discussed proposals to raise the retirement age from 60 to 65 to bridge pension coverage gaps while safeguarding youth employment opportunities.

The two sides discussed expanding bilateral tourism — buoyed by the growing popularity of K-pop in Sri Lanka — and noted the economic benefits of technical and vocational training gained by Sri Lankan youth working in South Korea.

The Korean delegation included CPE member Kwak Sang-eon, Korea-Sri Lanka Parliamentary Friendship Association Vice President Kim So-hee, and South Korean Ambassador to Sri Lanka Youn-Jung Kim. Secretary General of Parliament Kushani Rohanadeera also attended the meeting. (Colombo/Nov16/2026)

item.title: Abans Sept quarter net profit falls 28-pct to Rs791mn on finance costs
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: Surging borrowing costs and weaker associate earnings outweighed strong top-line growth
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT — Sri Lanka consumer durables and financial services group Abans PLC recorded a net profit of Rs. 790.6 million for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, down 28.4 percent from Rs. 1.10 billion a year earlier, as surging borrowing costs and weaker associate earnings outweighed strong top-line growth.

Basic earnings per share declining to Rs. 0.31 from Rs. 0.46, interim accounts showed.

Quarterly revenue jumped 30.8 percent to Rs. 19.81 billion from Rs. 15.15 billion, propelled by robust demand across its core trading and financial services operations.

Cost of sales rose at a slower 27.2 percent to Rs. 12.37 billion, lifting gross profit 37.2 percent to Rs. 7.44 billion and widening gross margins to 37.6 percent from 35.8 percent.

However, operating profit growth moderated to 25.5 percent, reaching Rs. 2.02 billion compared to Rs. 1.61 billion previously, as selling and distribution expenses surged 53.2 percent to Rs. 3.08 billion and administrative costs rose 29.5 percent to Rs. 2.44 billion amid retail expansion and higher warranty provisions.

Net profit was dragged down below the operating line by a 63.8 percent spike in finance costs to Rs. 998.7 million (from Rs. 609.8 million) and a 25.7 percent drop in finance income to Rs. 147.9 million.

Group interest-bearing borrowings expanded 45.3 percent from March 2026 to Rs. 38.41 billion — led by a 51.1 percent jump in short-term debt to Rs. 30.84 billion — to fund a 43.8 percent inventory buildup to Rs. 26.21 billion and higher receivables.

Share of profits from equity-accounted investees, Abans Electricals PLC and Colombo City Centre, plunged 62.7 percent to Rs. 103.3 million from Rs. 277.2 million.

Pre-tax profit declined 17.4 percent to Rs. 1.13 billion after financial services value-added tax rose 34.6 percent to Rs. 136.1 million, while income tax expense climbed 28.0 percent to Rs. 342.3 million.

Notes to the accounts disclosed a Rs. 1 billion term loan borrowed from associate Abans Electricals PLC, Rs. 1.34 billion raised in listed debentures via Abans Finance PLC, and a Rs. 466 million surcharge tax provision for 2020/21 settled after September 30. No new business ventures were announced.

Total group assets crossed Rs. 101.76 billion, with net asset value per share at Rs. 12.94 and debt-to-equity at 1.24 times. Abans PLC’s ordinary shares are not publicly traded, being wholly owned by Abans Retail Holdings (Pvt) Ltd. (Colombo/Nov16/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka taxman to issue valuation rules for crypto and gems under expanded capital gains tax
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: The 2027 budget proposes adding digital and virtual assets — including cryptocurrencies — alongside telecom and broadcas
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s Inland Revenue Department (IRD) will introduce formal valuation guidelines for calculating capital gains tax on cryptocurrencies, broadcast licenses, gems, and real estate after the 2027 budget expanded the tax net to cover digital and intangible assets.

Speaking at a Deloitte Sri Lanka post-budget webinar, IRD Senior Deputy Commissioner Nihal Wijewardena admitted that the lack of official valuation rules has caused widespread disputes over the September 30, 2017 baseline market value even for land and buildings.

Under existing tax law, capital gains tax applies mainly to land, buildings, and company shares, taxed at a concessionary 15 percent rate for individuals and 30 percent for companies.

The 2027 budget proposes adding digital and virtual assets — including cryptocurrencies — alongside telecom and broadcasting licenses, gems, jewelry, and precious metals to the definition of taxable capital assets.

Wijewardena said the upcoming tax amendment will give the Commissioner General legal authority to set clear valuation methods for each asset class.

“Definitely this time the provision will grant power to the Commissioner to issue a specific guideline when the amendment act is in operation,” Wijewardena said.

Tax practitioners at the forum noted that valuing volatile virtual assets or historic intangible rights could be even harder than pricing property unless clear rules are published before enforcement begins.

Wijewardena also clarified new anti-avoidance rules proposed for corporate amalgamations and mergers.

Currently, Sri Lanka’s tax laws contain no specific provisions governing company mergers, creating uncertainty over whether merged firms can carry forward past business losses.

While business groups raised concerns that anti-avoidance rules could penalize legitimate corporate restructurings, Wijewardena said the department aims to protect genuine commercial mergers as tax-neutral transactions while blocking artificial group arrangements designed solely to absorb tax losses.

“If the first reason for the amalgamation is business we can accept, if the first reason is tax avoidance then those should be answered,” he said.

Deloitte panelists urged the tax authority to consult the private sector before drafting the merger rules so complex business deals are not accidentally blocked.

Meanwhile, Wijewardena acknowledged that clearing overdue income tax refunds remains the single most important service standard the public should hold the IRD accountable for in 2027.

Following the abolition of the Simplified Value Added Tax (SVAT) system and the launch of a risk-based refund mechanism, the department cut average refund processing times to 29 days—against a 45-day legal limit—and cleared 7 billion rupees in decade-old arrears.

The 2027 budget also grants new export-oriented firms with at least 80 percent export turnover access to the fast-track VAT refund scheme after six months of registration, while giving legal recognition to electronic tax invoices. (Colombo/Nov16/2026)
